doc.title: Warren Vaché interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 23, 1995

chapter: Naming the music, family and Bix
title: Musical family and why not rock and roll
summary: Vaché's father was a bass player with a big 78 collection; he explains why rock never appealed to him.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Well, when you were in your teens, the rock thing was happening, right?
And what led you into this thing? Was it just by virtue of the fact that you played the cornet or the trumpet that you — or did you come from a musical —

I came from a musical family. Dad was a bass player and a part time musician who always worked doing casual jobs, what we used to call club dates, weddings, that sort of thing. He had a large record collection, and played records. One of my fondest memories as a kid is being able to wake up and lay in bed and listen to music for an hour. You know, it just was there. It was always around me. And Dad had a magnificent collection of 78s which he didn’t mind, you know, an eight or a nine year old going through and playing for himself. So these things were interesting, and I was interested in it. The reason I never really gravitated toward rock & roll was in part a snobishness on my part because I didn’t think it as interesting as the stuff I was listening to. And also in part it was not as interesting. I mean I still can’t take the Beach Boys as seriously as I can take Louis Armstrong, you know, or for that matter even Ray Noble, guys that were serious musicians. There was a lot of deep intent and thought put into music, and I didn’t find that in rock & roll.
